keyVerseText: Unto whom the prince of the eunuchs gave names: for he gave unto Daniel the name of Belteshazzar; and to Hananiah, of Shadrach; and to Mishael, of Meshach; and to Azariah, of Abednego.
rootMeaning: The name עֲבֵד נְגוֹ (ʻĂbêd Nᵉgôw) literally means "servant of Nebo," with Nebo being a Babylonian deity. This reflects the Babylonian practice of renaming captives to signify ownership or allegiance to their gods. The root form עֲבֵד נְגוֹא confirms this meaning and highlights the cultural and religious imposition on the Hebrew youth taken into exile, emphasizing the tension between their Godly identity and their Babylonian environment.
usageInScripture: This proper name occurs only once in Scripture, specifically in Daniel 1:7, where it is used as the Babylonian name given to Azariah. The consistent translation as "of Abednego" or simply "Abednego" shows that the term functions primarily as a personal name rather than a common noun, preserving the historical and narrative context of Daniel and his companions' experience in Babylonian captivity.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding עֲבֵד נְגוֹ as "servant of Nebo" deepens our appreciation of the spiritual challenges faced by Daniel's companions, who were pressured to abandon their faith and identity. Despite bearing a name that honors a pagan god, Abednego remained faithful to the God of Israel, illustrating the power of divine grace to preserve believers amid hostile cultures. This name reminds Christians that faithfulness to God transcends external circumstances and imposed identities, encouraging steadfastness in the face of trials.
keyVerseReflection: Daniel 1:7 records the renaming of Daniel and his three companions by the prince of the eunuchs, including Azariah being called Abednego. This verse highlights how the captives were given Babylonian names to assimilate them culturally and religiously. The use of עֲבֵד נְגוֹ here underscores the tension between their God-given identities and the foreign names imposed upon them, setting the stage for their courageous refusal to forsake God's commands despite external pressures.
